title: Brooks' Law
eyebrow: The 75-second case · adding people to a late project
lede: We're behind, so we doubled the team. Fred Brooks ran IBM's OS/360 and wrote down why that so often makes the date worse: every pair of people is a path that must stay in sync, and the paths grow much faster than the team.

monday.q: Before you add people: who trains them, and how does the work split again?
monday.honest: Paths count possible pairs, not meetings. Early, splittable work can take more people.

sources: Brooks, Frederick P., Jr. The Mythical Man-Month: Essays on Software Engineering. Reading, MA: Addison-Wesley, 1975. ISBN 0-201-00650-2. Preface (OS/360 from 1964); Ch. 2 (n(n−1)/2, Brooks's Law, the 12 man-month example, Figs. 2.5–2.8); Ch. 3 (OS/360: over 1,000 people at the peak; about 5,000 man-years, 1963–1966).
Brooks, Frederick P., Jr. The Mythical Man-Month, Anniversary Edition. Reading, MA: Addison-Wesley, 1995. ISBN 0-201-83595-9. Ch. 19, The Mythical Man-Month after 20 Years.
Abdel-Hamid, Tarek K., and Stuart E. Madnick. Software Project Dynamics: An Integrated Approach. Englewood Cliffs, NJ: Prentice Hall, 1991. ISBN 0-13-822040-9.
McConnell, Steve. “Brooks' Law Repealed?” IEEE Software 16, no. 6 (November/December 1999).
honest: Paths count possible pairs, not meetings. Real teams have structure, and Brooks himself called the law an outrageous oversimplification (1975), and in 1995 still “the best zeroth-order approximation to the truth”.

The 12 man-month grid is Brooks's own worked example from Chapter 2, not measured OS/360 data. The book gives OS/360's scale (over 1,000 people at the peak, about 5,000 man-years) but no figures for people added and months slipped; the film does not claim any.

Simulations (Abdel-Hamid and Madnick 1991) and McConnell (1999) find the law bites hardest late in a project with tightly coupled work; people added early, or to work that splits cleanly, can shorten it. 499,500 is our arithmetic on Brooks's peak figure: possible pairs among 1,000 people.
